result.markdown: # Tutorial 1: Evidence and probability foundations {#b-ep01 .unnumbered} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Tutorial 1, you can - classify variables and apply probability rules to a real dataset, - calculate expectations, variances, and quartiles from small distributions and tables, - interpret R output and correct the errors in an AI answer. ::: Tutorials are exam preparation sessions. The tasks below are exam-style questions. Attempt each task before you open its answer. You may use AI, following Attempt, Ask, Verify, Explain. ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Bring your after-class work from Lectures 1 to 3. Without looking at the chapters again, complete these definitions: 1. An observational unit is ... 2. An event is ... 3. A random variable is ... 4. A PMF is ... 5. The variance of a random variable averages ... 6. The lower quartile $Q_1$ and the upper quartile $Q_3$ are ... Use the [formula sheet](formula-sheet.qmd) up to and including Lecture 3. Review [Mathematics Refresher: sets and event notation](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#sets-and-event-notation) and [summation notation](../resources/math-refresher.qmd#summation-notation) if the notation is difficult for you. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation 1. An observational unit is the unit that one row of the data describes. 2. An event is a specified subset of the sample space. 3. A random variable is a numerical measurement of the outcome: a fixed rule that turns each outcome into a number. 4. A PMF assigns probability $P(X=x)$ to each value in the support of a discrete random variable. Its masses are non-negative and sum to 1. 5. Variance averages squared deviations from the variable's mean: $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E\!\left[(X-E[X])^2\right]$. 6. At least one quarter of the observations are at or below $Q_1$, and at least three quarters are at or above it. At least three quarters of the observations are at or below $Q_3$, and at least one quarter are at or above it. The difference $Q_3-Q_1$ is the interquartile range. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In the tutorial A complete written answer names the quantity and shows the calculation. It reports the value and units and interprets the value in context. It also states one important limit of the model or of the measurement. More tasks to practise at home are in the final section of this page, [Extra practice for home](#b-ep01-home). Tasks 1, 3, and 4 and the individual practice after class use the Shark Tank teaching file. Tasks 2 and 5 to 7 use invented examples. Load the file once: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) ``` ::: ### Task 1: Data and measurement [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} R reports: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rows columns min_description_words median_description_words 1 1441 19 1 5 max_description_words 1 13 ``` ::: ::: 1. What is the observational unit of the Shark Tank file? 2. Say in one sentence what is wrong with this claim: "The data contain 1,441 successful companies." 3. The variable `description_words` counts the words in the short written description of each pitch. Explain in one sentence what the median of 5 words tells you, and why the few descriptions of 12 or 13 words do not change it. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer 1. One row is one recorded televised pitch. 2. "Successful companies" is incorrect: the outcome is a deal made on the show, not completed funding or later venture performance. 3. At least half of the written descriptions have 5 words or fewer, and at least half have 5 words or more. The median depends only on the middle of the ordered values, so it stays at 5 however long the few longest descriptions are. ::: ### Task 2: Variables and samples A coffee-bar start-up records, for each of 150 orders: `order_id`, `drink` (espresso, latte, or tea), `cup_size` (small, medium, or large), `items` (the number of items), and `amount_eur` (the amount paid, in euros). 1. State the type of each variable: categorical (nominal or ordinal), numerical (discrete or continuous), or identifier. 2. The founder asks 150 loyalty-card holders whether they would pay more for oat milk. Is the main problem sampling variability or selection bias? Explain in two sentences. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer 1. `order_id` is an identifier, `drink` is categorical and nominal, `cup_size` is categorical and ordinal, `items` is numerical and discrete, and `amount_eur` is numerical and continuous. 2. The main problem is selection bias. Loyalty-card holders are regular customers who like the bar, so they may be more willing to pay extra than other customers. Asking more card holders would not fix this, because the sample was not drawn at random from all customers. ::: ### Task 3: Events and probability rules [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The event $D$ is an on-air deal. The event $M$ is that more than one entrepreneur presented the pitch (`multiple_entrepreneurs` equal to 1). This variable has no value for 427 pitches, so the experiment selects one of the 1,014 records with a value at random, each with the same probability. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} team <- sharks[!is.na(sharks$multiple_entrepreneurs), ] D <- team$deal_on_show == 1 # on-air deal M <- team$multiple_entrepreneurs == 1 # more than one entrepreneur ``` ::: R reports the counts of the 1,014 records: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` more_than_one on_air_deal no yes no 242 147 yes 309 316 ``` ::: ::: 1. Define the sample space $\Omega$. Then explain the difference between an outcome and the event $D$. 2. Translate $D^c$, $D\cap M$, and $D\cup M$ into words. 3. Calculate $P(D^c)$. 4. Calculate $P(D\cup M)$ using the addition rule. 5. Explain in one or two sentences why these probabilities do not automatically apply to a future US entrepreneur. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer 1. The sample space is the set of 1,014 pitch records with a value for `multiple_entrepreneurs`. One selected record is an outcome, while $D$ is the subset of $309+316=625$ deal records. 2. The complement $D^c$ is no on-air deal. The intersection $D\cap M$ is a deal for a pitch by more than one entrepreneur. The union $D\cup M$ is a deal, a pitch by more than one entrepreneur, or both. 3. $P(D^c)=(242+147)/1014=389/1014\approx0.384$. 4. With $P(D)=625/1014\approx0.616$, $P(M)=(147+316)/1014=463/1014\approx0.457$ and $P(D\cap M)=316/1014\approx0.312$, the addition rule gives $$ P(D\cup M)=\frac{625+463-316}{1014}=\frac{772}{1014}\approx0.761. $$ About three in four of these records end in a deal, come from a team, or both. 5. To use these probabilities for a future entrepreneur, you need a defined target population and a comparable selection, time period, and outcome. The 427 pitches without a value may also differ from the others. ::: ### Task 4: PMF, CDF, and expectation [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Select one of the 1,441 records at random, each with the same probability. Let $X=1$ if the founders offered at least 20% of their company to the sharks (`equity_offered_pct` of 20 or more) and $X=0$ otherwise. R counts these pitches: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` pitches offered_20_or_more proportion 1 1441 382 0.265 ``` ::: ::: Use $p=382/1441$. 1. Write the PMF and verify that its masses sum to 1. 2. Write the full piecewise CDF $F_X(a)$. 3. Calculate $E[X]$ from the PMF and interpret it in one sentence that compares it with the median offer in the file (10% of the company). 4. Explain why $E[X]$ equals the observed proportion of 1s. 5. Explain the difference between the random variable $X$ and a realised value $x=1$. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer 1. With $p=382/1441\approx0.265$ the PMF is $$ p_X(0)=1-p\approx0.735,\qquad p_X(1)=p\approx0.265, $$ and the masses sum to $1-p+p=1$. 2. The CDF is $$ F_X(a)= \begin{cases} 0,&a<0,\\ 1-p\approx0.735,&0\le a<1,\\ 1,&a\ge1. \end{cases} $$ 3. The expectation is $E[X]=0(1-p)+1p=p\approx0.265$. About one pitch in four offers at least 20% of the company. The median offer in the file is 10%, so these founders give away at least twice the typical share. 4. The indicator contains 382 ones among 1,441 observations, so its sum is 382 and its mean is $382/1441$, the proportion of 1s. 5. $X$ is the random variable: a numerical measurement of the outcome, a fixed rule that turns each selected pitch into a number (1 for an offer of at least 20%, 0 otherwise). $x=1$ is one realised value, the number obtained when the selected pitch offers 20% or more. ::: ### Task 5: Variance from a small PMF A venture studio models $N$, the number of investors who make an offer to one of its start-ups, with the PMF | $n$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | |---|---:|---:|---:| | $p_N(n)$ | 0.5 | 0.3 | 0.2 | 1. Calculate $E[N]$. 2. Calculate $\operatorname{Var}(N)$ from the definition $E\!\left[(N-E[N])^2\right]$. 3. Verify the result with the computational form $E[N^2]-\left(E[N]\right)^2$. 4. Report the standard deviation with its unit, and state in one sentence what it measures here. 5. Each offer costs the studio 3 hours of meetings, and every start-up needs 2 hours of preparation. The time spent on one start-up is therefore $T=3N+2$ hours. Calculate $E[T]$ and $\operatorname{SD}(T)$. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check a model answer 1. $E[N]=0(0.5)+1(0.3)+2(0.2)=0.7$ offers. 2. Definition form: $$ \operatorname{Var}(N)=(0-0.7)^2(0.5)+(1-0.7)^2(0.3)+(2-0.7)^2(0.2) =0.245+0.027+0.338=0.61. $$ 3. Computational form: $E[N^2]=0^2(0.5)+1^2(0.3)+2^2(0.2)=1.1$, so $\operatorname{Var}(N)=1.1-0.7^2=1.1-0.49=0.61$. The two methods agree. 4. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{0.61}\approx0.78$ offers. It measures the typical distance of the realised number of offers from the mean of 0.7, in the original unit (offers), whereas the variance is in squared offers. 5. Time per start-up: use the rules for $aX+b$ with $a=3$ and $b=2$. $E[T]=3E[N]+2=3\times0.7+2=4.1$ hours. $\operatorname{SD}(T)=|3|\operatorname{SD}(N)\approx3\times0.78=2.34$ hours, more than half of the expected time. The 2 hours of preparation raise the expected time and leave the spread unchanged. ::: ### Task 6: Check the AI You asked an AI assistant about the number of offers $N$ in Task 5. It answered: > "E[N] = 0.7, so most start-ups get 0.7 offers. The variance is 0.61, so the > number of offers typically differs from 0.7 by 0.61 offers." The answer contains two errors. Check it sentence by sentence and name each error in one sentence. Then write the corrected answer in at most three sentences. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The first sentence is wrong. No start-up gets 0.7 offers, because $N$ is a count with the values 0, 1, and 2. The expected value is a probability-weighted average, not the most likely value. The most likely number is 0 offers, with probability 0.5. The second sentence is also wrong. The variance 0.61 is in squared offers. The typical distance from 0.7 is the standard deviation, $\sqrt{0.61}\approx0.78$ offers. Corrected answer: on average a start-up gets 0.7 offers, half of the start-ups get no offer, and the number of offers typically differs from 0.7 by about 0.78 offers. ::: ### Task 7: Two options, compared by expected value and spread Two founders sell second-hand designer clothes online. For December they want to rent a pop-up store, and they can choose between two locations. Option A is a shop in a side street of the city centre. Option B is a booth at the Christmas market, where the rent is high and the number of visitors depends on the weather. $X$ is the profit of the month with option A and $Y$ is the profit of the month with option B, both in thousands of euros. A negative value is a loss. The founders use these two PMFs: | $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | $p_X(x)$ | 0.05 | 0.25 | 0.45 | 0.15 | 0.10 | | $y$ | $-2$ | 0 | 2 | 4 | 8 | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | $p_Y(y)$ | 0.10 | 0.10 | 0.20 | 0.50 | 0.10 | 1. Check that both tables are valid PMFs. 2. Calculate $E[X]$ and $E[Y]$. 3. Calculate $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ from the definition $E\!\left[(X-E[X])^2\right]$. 4. Verify both variances with the computational form $E[X^2]-\left(E[X]\right)^2$. 5. Calculate both standard deviations and state them in euros. Compare each standard deviation with the expected profit of its option. 6. Calculate the probability of a loss for each option. 7. Decide which option you would choose. Give three numbers that support your choice (the expected profits, the standard deviations, and the probabilities of a loss) and one sentence on the founders' attitude to risk. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer 1. No mass is negative. The masses sum to 1 in both tables: $0.05+0.25+0.45+0.15+0.10=1$ and $0.10+0.10+0.20+0.50+0.10=1$. 2. The expected profits are $$ \begin{aligned} E[X]&=0(0.05)+1(0.25)+2(0.45)+3(0.15)+4(0.10)\\ &=0+0.25+0.90+0.45+0.40=2.0,\\ E[Y]&=(-2)(0.10)+0(0.10)+2(0.20)+4(0.50)+8(0.10)\\ &=-0.20+0+0.40+2.00+0.80=3.0, \end{aligned} $$ that is 2,000 euros for option A and 3,000 euros for option B. 3. Definition form: $$ \operatorname{Var}(X)=(0-2)^2(0.05)+(1-2)^2(0.25)+(2-2)^2(0.45)+ (3-2)^2(0.15)+(4-2)^2(0.10) $$ $$ =0.20+0.25+0+0.15+0.40=1.00, $$ $$ \operatorname{Var}(Y)=(-2-3)^2(0.10)+(0-3)^2(0.10)+(2-3)^2(0.20)+ (4-3)^2(0.50)+(8-3)^2(0.10) $$ $$ =2.50+0.90+0.20+0.50+2.50=6.60. $$ 4. Computational form: $$ \begin{aligned} E[X^2]&=0(0.05)+1(0.25)+4(0.45)+9(0.15)+16(0.10)\\ &=0+0.25+1.80+1.35+1.60=5.00,\\ E[Y^2]&=4(0.10)+0(0.10)+4(0.20)+16(0.50)+64(0.10)\\ &=0.40+0+0.80+8.00+6.40=15.60, \end{aligned} $$ so $\operatorname{Var}(X)=5.00-2^2=1.00$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=15.60-3^2=6.60$. Both forms agree. 5. $\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{1.00}=1.00$ thousand euros, that is 1,000 euros. This is half of the expected profit of option A. $\operatorname{SD}(Y)=\sqrt{6.60}\approx2.57$ thousand euros, that is about 2,570 euros. This is about 86% of the expected profit of option B. 6. Option A has no negative value, so $P(X<0)=0$. For option B, $P(Y<0)=p_Y(-2)=0.10$. 7. Both choices can be correct if the numbers support the reason. Option B has the higher expected profit, 3,000 against 2,000 euros (50% more). Option A has the smaller standard deviation, 1,000 against about 2,570 euros. Option A never makes a loss, while option B loses 2,000 euros with probability 0.10. Founders who dislike risk choose option A because a loss would put the venture in danger, while founders who can afford such a loss choose option B for its higher expected profit. The code below checks these results in R. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x_val <- 0:4 x_prob <- c(0.05, 0.25, 0.45, 0.15, 0.10) y_val <- c(-2, 0, 2, 4, 8) y_prob <- c(0.10, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50, 0.10) mean_x <- sum(x_val * x_prob) mean_y <- sum(y_val * y_prob) c(E_X = mean_x, E_Y = mean_y, Var_X_definition = sum((x_val - mean_x)^2 * x_prob), Var_X_shortcut = sum(x_val^2 * x_prob) - mean_x^2, Var_Y_definition = sum((y_val - mean_y)^2 * y_prob), Var_Y_shortcut = sum(y_val^2 * y_prob) - mean_y^2, SD_X = sqrt(sum((x_val - mean_x)^2 * x_prob)), SD_Y = sqrt(sum((y_val - mean_y)^2 * y_prob)), P_loss_X = sum(x_prob[x_val < 0]), P_loss_Y = sum(y_prob[y_val < 0])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` E_X E_Y Var_X_definition Var_X_shortcut 2.000000 3.000000 1.000000 1.000000 Var_Y_definition Var_Y_shortcut SD_X SD_Y 6.600000 6.600000 1.000000 2.569047 P_loss_X P_loss_Y 0.000000 0.100000 ``` ::: ::: The output repeats the results by hand: the expected profits 2 and 3, both forms of each variance (1 and 6.6), the standard deviations 1 and about 2.57, and the loss probabilities 0 and 0.10. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class ### Individual practice [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The R output below describes the amount of money the founders asked for (`ask_amount_usd`, in US dollars) in the Shark Tank file: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean median minimum maximum 283510.8 200000.0 10000.0 5000000.0 ``` ::: ::: Write no more than 100 words. Compare mean and median, calculate the range, and say what the variable does and does not measure. Then explain which value equals the expectation if every record gets probability $1/1441$. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check a model answer The founders asked for 283,511 dollars on average, while the median ask is 200,000 dollars. The mean is about 42% above the median, because a few very large asks pull it up: the distribution is right-skewed. The range is $5{,}000{,}000-10{,}000=4{,}990{,}000$ dollars, so the largest ask is 500 times the smallest. If each record gets probability $1/1441$, the expectation of this distribution is the mean, about 283,511 dollars. The variable measures the amount asked on the show, not the amount the sharks agreed to invest or the money the venture finally received. ::: ### Check your understanding Complete from memory: 1. An event is ... 2. A PMF must ... 3. A CDF at $a$ reports ... 4. Expectation is ... 5. Variance is ... and its square root is ... ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. An event is a specified subset of the sample space. 2. A PMF is non-negative and sums to 1 over the support. 3. $F_X(a)=P(X\le a)$. 4. $E[X]=\sum_x x\, p_X(x)$, the probability-weighted average of the possible values. 5. Variance is the probability-weighted average of squared deviations from the mean, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-\left(E[X]\right)^2$. Its square root is the standard deviation, in the variable's original unit. ::: ### Make it yours :::: {.utility-prompt} Two sentences about your own venture Think of your own venture, or any business you know well. Pick one uncertain count that matters for it, for example customers who sign up in a week, offers received, or orders returned. Write two sentences. First, sketch a small PMF for the count: three or four values with rough probabilities. Then say what its expectation and standard deviation would tell you about a real decision. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## See an example, then write your own Take a student-run campus venture that sells boxes of prepared meals. "Weekly catering requests: 0 with probability 0.4, 1 with 0.4, 2 with 0.15, and 3 with 0.05, so I expect about 0.85 requests per week. The standard deviation tells me whether a weekend helper is justified. With a high spread, some weeks need a helper even though the average says no." ::: You can discuss this task, and any other task in this tutorial, with [Tilly for QM Basic](https://chatbot.tilburg.ai/chat?token=b8500619-4e8e-488e-9a44-b2e5dbf40d2f), the course AI assistant. :::: ### More practice For extra exercises on the lectures of this tutorial, with worked solutions, ask Tilly for QM Basic, the course AI assistant. For example: "Give me an extra exercise for Tutorial 1. Show the solution only after I send my answer." ### Extra practice for home {#b-ep01-home} These tasks practise the calculations of Lectures 1 to 3 at home. All four use invented examples. You need a simple calculator and the formula sheet. #### Task 8: Read a histogram A venture records the delivery times of 120 orders. @fig-bep01-delivery groups them into intervals of 10 minutes, and each bar includes its upper limit. The number above each bar is its count. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) delivery <- data.frame( midpoint = c(5, 15, 25, 35, 45), # middle of each 10-minute interval orders = c(18, 46, 32, 16, 8) ) ggplot(delivery, aes(x = midpoint, y = orders)) + geom_col(width = 10, fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.85, colour = "white") + geom_text(aes(label = orders), vjust = -0.5, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.6) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 50, by = 10)) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) + labs(x = "Delivery time (minutes)", y = "Number of orders") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Delivery times of 120 orders (invented example), in intervals of 10 minutes. Each bar includes its upper limit. The number above a bar is its count.](t01-exam-prep_files/figure-html/fig-bep01-delivery-1.png){#fig-bep01-delivery fig-alt='Histogram with five bars over delivery times from 0 to 50 minutes. The counts are 18 for 0 to 10 minutes, 46 for above 10 up to 20, 32 for above 20 up to 30, 16 for above 30 up to 40, and 8 for above 40 up to 50.' width=672} ::: ::: 1. What does one observation represent, and what is on each axis? 2. Describe the tallest bar in one full sentence. 3. Which interval contains the median? Show the cumulative counts. 4. Which interval contains the upper quartile $Q_3$? Use the cumulative counts again. 5. Describe the shape, and state one thing the histogram cannot tell you. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer 1. One observation is one order. The horizontal axis is the delivery time in minutes and the vertical axis is the number of orders. 2. The tallest bar: 46 orders took more than 10 and at most 20 minutes. 3. With 120 orders the median lies between the 60th and the 61st ordered value. The cumulative counts are 18 and then 18 + 46 = 64, so both values lie in the second interval: the median delivery time is above 10 and at most 20 minutes. 4. Three quarters of 120 orders is 90, so $Q_3$ lies at the 90th and the 91st ordered value. The cumulative counts are 18, 64, and then 64 + 32 = 96. Both values lie in the third interval: $Q_3$ is above 20 and at most 30 minutes, so at least three quarters of the orders arrive within 30 minutes. 5. The distribution is right-skewed: most orders arrive within 30 minutes and a few take much longer. The histogram cannot say which orders were late or why, and it hides the exact times inside each interval. ::: #### Task 9: Mean, spread, and quartiles from a frequency table A founder runs an escape room. Groups of 2 to 6 persons book the room for one hour. The table shows the group size of the 40 bookings of last week. | Group size (persons) | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Number of bookings | 4 | 12 | 10 | 8 | 6 | Give every booking the same weight, $1/40$. This is the empirical distribution of Lecture 3, so the relative frequencies work like a PMF. 1. State what one observation is. Calculate the relative frequency of each group size and check that the five values sum to 1. 2. Calculate the mean group size. 3. Calculate the variance and the standard deviation of this empirical distribution. Use the variance formula of Lecture 3 with the relative frequencies as weights. This version divides by $n$. State the unit. Then calculate the sample standard deviation $s$ of Lecture 3, which divides by $n-1$. 4. Write down the cumulative counts and find the median. 5. Find the lower quartile $Q_1$ and the upper quartile $Q_3$ with cumulative counts, as for the median in Lecture 1. Add the counts from the left until the running total first reaches one quarter of the observations. The group size at which this happens is $Q_1$. Do the same with three quarters for $Q_3$. Then calculate the interquartile range and interpret it in one sentence. 6. Compare the mean with the median. What does the comparison say about the shape of the distribution? For these 40 values, R's `quantile()` reports the same median and the same quartiles as the rules in parts 4 and 5. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer 1. One observation is one booking. The relative frequencies are $4/40=0.10$, $12/40=0.30$, $10/40=0.25$, $8/40=0.20$, and $6/40=0.15$. Their sum is 1. 2. The mean is $$ 2(0.10)+3(0.30)+4(0.25)+5(0.20)+6(0.15)=0.20+0.90+1.00+1.00+0.90=4.0 $$ persons. The counts give the same result: $$ \frac{2\times4+3\times12+4\times10+5\times8+6\times6}{40}=\frac{160}{40}=4.0. $$ 3. The variance is $$ (2-4)^2(0.10)+(3-4)^2(0.30)+(4-4)^2(0.25)+(5-4)^2(0.20)+(6-4)^2(0.15) $$ $$ =0.40+0.30+0+0.20+0.60=1.50. $$ The standard deviation is $\sqrt{1.50}\approx1.22$ persons. A booking typically differs from the mean of 4 persons by about 1.2 persons, which is about 31% of the mean. This variance divides by $n=40$. The sum of the squared deviations is $40\times1.50=60$. The sample variance divides it by $n-1=39$: $s^2=60/39\approx1.54$ and $s\approx1.24$ persons, the value of R's `sd()`. 4. The cumulative counts are 4, 16, 26, 34, and 40. With 40 observations the median is the average of the 20th and the 21st ordered value. The ordered values 17 to 26 all have group size 4, so the median is 4 persons. 5. One quarter of 40 is 10. The running total first reaches 10 at group size 3, because $16\ge10$, so $Q_1=3$. Three quarters of 40 is 30. The running total first reaches 30 at group size 5, because $34\ge30$, so $Q_3=5$. The interquartile range is $5-3=2$ persons: the middle half of the bookings lies between 3 and 5 persons. Of the 40 bookings, 16 are at or below 3 persons. That is 40%, more than one quarter, which is why the definition of $Q_1$ says "at least one quarter". 6. The mean and the median are both 4 persons, so the two agree. The distribution has no long tail on one side that pulls the mean away from the median.
